Text.Text: You wear the bloom better than I did. I check, some nights. Keep the rules closer than the blades, and don't go back down for applause. There's nothing else I can teach you.

Show me your hands. ...Almost. Almost is what the backrooms bury. When the two blades stop being two thoughts -- when there's nothing left of the paired work you haven't taken all the way -- come find me.

What are you willing to bleed? Think before you answer. Behind the main pit there's a sealed door into the backrooms. Past it, people fight with my form and none of my rules. Six of their students are cutting their way toward dangerous. Stop all six. Their teachers keep a coded bout ledger -- the Backroom Bout Ledger. Bring it to me. The key I'm giving you fits the door. Nothing else about this will be given.
Good answer. Short. The door behind the main pit takes your key. Six students, then the ledger. It comes back readable -- don't bleed on the pages.
Two cuts. They open together, or they're just cuts. Most people spend a career teaching two blades to agree. The bloom is what happens after they stop needing to. That's all I'll say standing up.

Mine, once removed. Someone in the backrooms taught my form from watching my old bouts. Kept the shape. Dropped the rules. The rules were the part that cost me something. Six students so far. There will be sixty if the school stays open.
Names. Odds. Which bouts were fixed to end in a funeral. I left the circuit so my form would stop filling graves. The ledger will tell me how far behind I already am.
Six, and the ledger. Count them yourself. The backrooms won't count for you.
You're moving differently. Slower. Good -- that's the weight of doing it right. The ledger.
Thirty-one bouts. Nine marked to end wrong. You stopped six students; the school barely noticed. It will. Take your pay. Come back when your cuts have settled.

Five more. The ledger calls them specialists -- students who've bled long enough to teach. They fight in a pit wired through a ring shock regulator somebody rebuilt to keep downed fighters twitching for the crowd. Kill the five. Then tear the Ring Shock Regulator out of the wall. I want to hold what they made of my retirement.
Then go. The five won't leave the pits -- pride. The regulator hangs above the champion's pit. You'll want both hands free and no audience.
Like me, if you'd only ever seen me angry. They'll pair on you -- one high, one low, both patient. Don't watch the blades. Watch the feet. And never let two of them agree on a rhythm.

That regulator hung over my last title bout. It cut the current the instant I dropped my opponent -- saved her life. Someone rewired mercy into a goad. I'd like it back on my wall, ugly and honest. That's all.
A bout I won. The crowd wanted the second cut. I gave it. She was nineteen. That's the whole story anyone is owed, including you. My rules exist so it stays the only one.
Five specialists. Then the regulator off the wall above the champion's pit. In that order -- the current stays live while they're breathing.
Burns on your knuckles. You pulled it live. The regulator, then.

They soldered the mercy out of it. Cheap work. I'll rebuild it the way it hung in my day. You've cut the school's teachers out from under it -- which means the man at the deep gate knows your name now. Before you go near him, we talk. That's not a request.

The deep gate has a doorman. The backrooms call him the warden. He held my title for a season -- lost it to me, kept the crack I put in his pit sigil, and found a door worth guarding instead of a ring worth winning. He is better than everyone you've met down there put together. So. My one condition, the only one I have ever set: you do not face him alone. Two people you'd bleed for, at your sides, or you don't knock. Beat him. Bring me the Cracked Pit Sigil. I've owed it a proper burial for years.

Word taken. He'll open the gate himself -- he considers a knock a courtesy worth returning. When it's done, close his eyes and take the sigil. He'd rather it went to someone who earned it through him.

I broke his sigil with the last clean bloom I ever threw. He bowed. The crowd never understood that bow. He didn't keep the broken sigil out of shame -- he kept it as a promise that no one would pass him carelessly again. When you knock, he'll already know whose student you are.

Because he'd let me pass. Whatever's left of that circuit still bows to me, and a door that opens for your name proves nothing and fixes less. It has to be someone the backrooms owe nothing. And if I went down those stairs, I'm not sure which of us I'd be by the bottom.

One fighter is a rhythm. He has spent years ending rhythms -- it's all the door asks of him. Three of you is an argument. He can win any exchange. He can't win every exchange at once. Every name carved by that gate went down alone. I count them, some nights. Don't be a number I count.
The gate is still guarded. Two beside you -- that condition doesn't expire. The Cracked Pit Sigil comes home after.
I felt it from up here. Don't ask me how. Let me see the sigil.

Both cracks are mine, in a way. He was the best thing about that circuit and the last of my era standing. You did it right -- three shadows on the stairs, I checked. Rest. What's past that gate is the promoter's circle, and they don't fight for doors. They fight for pay.

Four left before the champion's room. The promoter's inner circle -- fighters paid to keep my form profitable and lawless. They taught the students, hired the specialists, and put a good man on a door to die. Kill all four. The last one standing carries the Promoter's Payout Chit -- hand-signed, because the promoter trusts nothing with a memory. That chit opens the champion's room. It is also every death he has purchased, in his own ink.
Then go collect. The circle drinks in the promoter's lounge past the warden's gate -- they'll be slower and meaner for it. The chit will be on whoever dies last. It's always on whoever dies last.

A counter-fighter who waits better than most people breathe. A pair who share one tempo -- kill the tempo, not the pair, whichever body you can reach first. And a big one who thinks pain is a currency he's rich in. They'll come staggered; the promoter pays per rescue. Keep your two close anyway. Staggered becomes together when money is dying.

My title. Someone is wearing it. She took my name off the boards and put the bloom back to work in the deep pit, the way the crowd always wanted it from me. I'm told she throws it red every night. Ask me the rest when the circle's dead. I'll answer. I keep my word slowly, but I keep it.

It goes to people on this moon who set odds and hate being lied to, with my statement attached. The backrooms exist because the money is invisible. The promoter's own hand makes it visible. I don't need him dead. I need him poor, and famous for the right things. Poor men can't rent pits.
Four fighters, then the chit off the final one. The champion's room stays sealed until the promoter's ink opens it.
You're not bleeding. They were the promoter's best and you're not bleeding. Show me the chit.

Good ink. Heavy hand. Frightened man. This closes every account but one -- the room where my title lives. Sit down before you ask. When you're ready to hear about her, I'll tell you all of it, and then you'll wish I hadn't.

Her name doesn't matter. She took mine. My last student. She watched me walk away from the title and decided the walking away was the flaw in the form. In the deep pit she throws the Red Bloom the way it always wanted to be thrown -- both cuts open, nothing held back. She is what I would be without the rules, which means I know exactly how this goes. Nobody has left her ring alone since she took it. Nobody. So my condition stands one last time, harder than before: two beside you, sworn, or the door stays shut. Kill her, and the bloom comes back clean. There is no trophy to bring me. Walking up the stairs is the proof.

Then it's set. She'll know you're coming -- she reads the backrooms the way I taught her to. It won't help her. Rhythm, distance, and two people who'd bleed for you. Come back up. That's the whole instruction.

You don't out-bloom her. She holds the full form -- the one you're here to earn -- and she spends lives keeping it sharp. So deny her the second cut. The bloom is two cuts agreeing; break the agreement. One of you takes the first, the other two answer before the second opens. She has never fought people who fight for each other. Down there, nobody does.

The best I ever trained, and the only one I ever refused to pass. She asked what I was willing to bleed, the day we met. Same thing I asked you. Her answer was everyone else. I should have ended it there. I gave her footwork instead. This is me paying that debt with your hands, and I know exactly what that makes me.

Then the form has no owner left but the two of us, and I'm retired. The rules come with it, whether you want them or not. You've been keeping them for five bouts already, mostly without noticing. That was the real trial. Her ring is just the last question on it.
The champion's room is open and she's still in it. Two sworn beside you -- if either hesitates on the stairs, turn around and wait for better. I'll know if you didn't.
The backrooms went quiet an hour ago. Real quiet, not held-breath quiet. Say it anyway. I want to hear it in a living voice.

Then it's yours. The form, the rules, the weight -- all of it, and I'm sorry for exactly one third of that. You did what I couldn't, and you did it clean: three went down and three came back up. That matters more than the title ever did. Go on. Don't visit. Champions who visit their old rings end up back in them.
Let me ask something else.
Whatever it costs. I'm in.
What is the Red Bloom?
Whose students are they?
What do you want with their ledger?
I don't have an answer yet.
Here. The whole book.
One more question.
Five, and the regulator. Done.
How will the specialists come at me?
Why does the regulator matter to you?
Why did you leave the circuit?
Not yet.
Off the wall. It's yours.
Back to the gate.
Two at my side. You have my word.
You know him?
Why not go yourself?
Why three of us? He's one man.
I don't have two people I'd trust with this. Not yet.
It's done. Here's his sigil.
Go back over the four.
Four. And I'll bring you his ink.
What should I know about the four?
Who's in the champion's room?
What happens to the chit after?
Soon. Not tonight.
The chit. His signature is on everything.
Go over it again.
Two sworn. Open the door.
How do I beat her form?
What was she to you?
And when it's over -- what then?
When my two are ready. Not before.
She's dead. The bloom is finished.
